lesson.text: Quick memory: why does your heart beat faster when you exercise? (Your muscles need more oxygen.) Today: the parts of fitness, and how to warm up and cool down.
Fitness has parts. Stamina: keeping going for a long time. Strength: pushing, pulling and lifting. Speed: moving fast. Flexibility: bending and stretching easily.
Different activities build different parts. Swimming lengths builds stamina, press-ups build strength, sprints build speed, and yoga stretches build flexibility. Many games build them all!
Warm up before exercise, in three parts: a pulse raiser, like gentle jogging, to warm your muscles and speed up your heart; then moving your joints, like arm circles; then moving stretches.
Cool down after exercise: slow down gently, like walking, so your heart and breathing slow down. Then hold still stretches for about 10 seconds each, gently, never bouncing.
Circuit training is a set of stations, each with a different exercise. Work at each one for, say, 30 seconds. 6 stations of 30 seconds is 6 × 30 = 180 seconds: 3 minutes.
Children should be active for at least 60 minutes a day on average. On at least 3 days a week, do things that make muscles and bones strong, like climbing, jumping and skipping.

Try it in the world: build a fitness trail with a station for each part: a long track for stamina, a climbing wall for strength, a sprint lane for speed and a stretching mat for flexibility. Then try a real one!

exercises.prompt: Match each part of fitness to its meaning.
exercises.hint: Think of a long jog, a climb, a sprint and a stretch.
exercises.explain: Stamina: keeping going. Strength: pushing, pulling, lifting. Speed: moving fast. Flexibility: bending and stretching.

exercises.prompt: Which part of fitness does a long, steady jog build most?
exercises.hint: A long jog is about keeping going.
exercises.explain: Stamina: a long, steady jog trains you to keep going for a long time.

exercises.prompt: You should warm up before exercise.
exercises.explain: True: a warm-up gets your heart, muscles and joints ready, so you move well and safely.

exercises.prompt: Which is a stretch for flexibility?
exercises.hint: Flexibility is about bending and stretching.
exercises.explain: Touching your toes gently stretches the backs of your legs: flexibility.

exercises.hint: Start gently, and warm your muscles before you stretch them.
items: gentle jogging to raise your pulse
exercises.explain: Pulse raiser first, then moving your joints, then moving stretches, then the main activity.

exercises.prompt: Why do we cool down slowly after exercise?
exercises.hint: What happens to your heart after a race?
choices: so the heart and breathing slow down gently
to make the heart beat faster
exercises.explain: A slow cool-down lets your heart and breathing come back down gently.

exercises.prompt: A circuit has 8 stations. You work for 30 seconds at each one. How many seconds is that?
exercises.hint: The same time at every station: multiply.

exercises.prompt: When you stretch, you should bounce to reach further.
exercises.hint: What does the lesson say about bouncing?
exercises.explain: False: stretch gently and hold still. Bouncing can hurt your muscles.

items: a gentle jog to raise your pulse
a slow walk at the end
slow, deep breaths at the end
exercises.hint: Is it getting you ready, or helping you slow down afterwards?
exercises.explain: Warm-up: jog, arm circles, knee lifts. Cool-down: slow walk, still stretches, slow breaths.

exercises.prompt: Zara wants to run further without stopping. Which part of fitness should she build?
exercises.hint: Running further is about keeping going.
exercises.explain: Stamina: long, steady runs help her keep going for longer.

exercises.prompt: Bram wants to reach his toes more easily. Which activity helps most?
exercises.hint: Reaching further is about bending and stretching.
exercises.explain: Gentle stretches every day build flexibility, little by little.

exercises.prompt: 6 stations of 40 seconds, with a 20 second rest between one station and the next. How many seconds from start to finish?
exercises.hint: There is one fewer rest than stations.

exercises.prompt: Children should be active for at least 60 minutes a day on average.
exercises.hint: Think of about an hour of being active.
exercises.explain: True: at least 60 minutes a day on average, across the week.

exercises.prompt: What does a pulse raiser do in a warm-up?
exercises.hint: The name tells you what it raises.
choices: warms the muscles and speeds up the heart
stretches the muscles as far as they go
exercises.explain: A pulse raiser, like gentle jogging, raises your pulse and warms your muscles.

exercises.prompt: Holding still stretches for about 10 seconds is part of a cool-down.
exercises.hint: What do you do after slowing down at the end?
exercises.explain: True: after slowing down, hold gentle still stretches.

exercises.prompt: Zara is active for 45 minutes on Monday, 70 on Tuesday and 65 on Wednesday. Share the total equally over the 3 days: how many minutes a day is that?
exercises.hint: Add the three days, then share the total into 3 equal parts.
exercises.explain: 45 + 70 + 65 = 180 minutes. Shared over 3 days: 180 ÷ 3 = 60 minutes a day, exactly the 60 minutes a day children should aim for on average.
